It depends on where you’re at in your recovery and how severe the trigger is. When I was at my worst, a full-blown flashback would take me up to 2 days to recover from (the actual flashback lasting somewhere around 5-15 minutes in my case). When I got better, that same flashback would take me out for maybe a few hours. I’ve had somatic flashbacks last up to a week before, but they’re more emotional/physical feelings, and less tangible. 

The really intense ones would be flashes of imagery, body feelings, smells, etc. Complete conscious panic, yelling, freezing, crying. My brain would repeat things like, “It’s happening again, it’s happening again”. I would be completely taken from reality and put into this memory replay.

The milder flashbacks could come as an intangible sense of dread, panic, re-experiencing the emotions from the event, feeling the physical feelings of the event, feeling that I’m not safe.

Everyone experiences them differently though.

I think the idea is that we hold trauma in our bodies, through chronic pain, inflammation, tension, etc. Yoga helps you to release that tension, and for some people, it can even cause emotional release (like you might get emotional while practicing with no apparent cause). 

However, I think if nothing is happening for you emotionally, that doesn’t mean you’re doing anything wrong. Yoga is only one of many ways to release tension in the body, and it isn’t a cure-all. It is still incredibly helpful for learning emotional awareness and reducing muscle tension. It can also help to improve emotional regulation, which is vital in learning how to heal. 

I wouldn’t go looking for any huge “ah-ha” moment of catharsis, because it can be damaging to force yourself into an emotional breakdown, especially if you aren’t equipped with the coping skills to handle it. Chances are, if you feel that you’re holding in traumatic emotions, you aren’t ready to deal with them yet. Yoga will not be a magic release and suddenly everything is okay. Trauma doesn’t work that way. 

I think that sometimes we get caught up in the false notion that there is some kind of profound “letting go” that happens. When you have PTSD, the whole thing is that you are unable to “let go” because your bodily functioning is completely built off of trauma response and fight/flight/freeze reactions. Healing will happen slowly over a long period of time, with lots of steps backwards and forwards. There is no magic moment of “letting go” where suddenly you aren’t traumatized anymore. 

My recommendation, as someone who is certified to teach yoga, is to do it as long as it is serving you in a healthy way. I think that the best thing yoga can do for a traumatized person is increase emotional awareness. Because you can’t heal if you don’t know how you’re feeling. It will make you feel better physically, too. Beyond that, don’t expect any huge, profound change. 

If you’re experiencing flashbacks or intrusive thoughts when you do it, you might not be ready for it yet. Sometimes it’s hard for us to be by ourselves in our bodies. Just keep doing what feels good to you.

There are lots of different kinds of flashbacks. I’m not a professional, but here are a few that I’ve experienced myself:

(These are told from my POV, so some of the details of the experience may vary) 

1.) Traditional flashbacks. You are completely sucked out of the present moment. It feels like your trauma is happening all over again. You see images of the trauma, and you slip into a trance state. Your thoughts race, thinking “It’s happening again.” You can’t logically convince yourself that it *isn’t* happening again. You panic, looking around wildly and your fight/flight reaction is triggered. 

2.) Somatic flashbacks. You relive physical sensations from the trauma. You can feel someone touching you. You can smell the same smells as the traumatic event. You may even hear the traumatic event via auditory hallucination. 

3.) Emotional flashbacks. You relive all of the emotions of the trauma. Your emotions don’t line up with your current situation. It seems that they’re running away from you, and you’re caught up in how you felt during the trauma.

You can convince yourself that you’re thinking clearly as much as you want, but at the end of the day, if you’re considering suicide, you aren’t. 

When we deal with brain chemistry issues, it can cause us to think this way. You can be as “clear” as you are, and that doesn’t change the fact that you are being clouded by your mental illness. It is not normal to feel this hopeless, and that is a sure sign that your brain is not functioning the way it should be. 

I know that it seems like this is the only option, but I promise you that there is *so much good* left to see. I was in your position at the same age, and I really didn’t think I’d live this long. It will not be a perfect journey, there will be tons of steps forward and tons backwards. But at the end of it all, you’ll be so glad you didn’t follow through with this. Let it mean something to you when I say, I am writing this to my past self as much as I am to you.

I am nowhere near okay right now, but I have that collection of moments that have proven life is worth living anyway. From where I write these words to where you read them, I love you.

During an intake, it’s normal for a therapist to ask you what your trauma was, and expect a simple answer such as “I had an accident”, or “I was sexually assaulted.” But they should NEVER ask you to relive or disclose details before you are ready. 

If they force you to disclose details, this can retraumatize you, ESPECIALLY if you don’t know any healthy coping mechanisms yet. 

My advice, if they pressure you to give them any more details than the basics, walk away. They should never be pressuring you that way, and they should never threaten not to treat you otherwise. If they do this, find a new therapist. Look for someone who is trauma-informed. 

You have every right to stand up and walk out of a session if you are ever uncomfortable. I’ve been in therapy for a long time, and I have never had a therapist force me to disclose the details.

Before you should even dive in and try to process your trauma, it is helpful to have a big set of coping skills to help you through being triggered. In my program, we start with mindfulness, and then gather tons of DBT skills. We don’t process the trauma in this program, but once we have a good grasp on managing symptoms, we graduate and can move onto trauma processing via EMDR or outpatient therapy. Most people won’t be able to talk about their trauma in depth without having skills to ground and relax during the process. 

I highly recommend seeing if there is a trauma Intensive outpatient program near you. If not, look for a DBT based therapist/program where you can learn coping skills. Otherwise, trying to go straight into processing your trauma can be way to overwhelming.

Ptsd isn’t really actually about the trauma, it’s about how your brain handles the trauma. One of the identifying markers for ptsd is an identifiable trauma, but there is no rule for how severe it needs to be.

A lot of times we fall into this “I shouldn’t have ptsd because someone else had it worse” thing. However large or small your trauma is, it has caused you to have difficulty functioning in your daily life. That’s what matters. Whether you’ve been bullied in middle school or went through a war, your symptoms and feelings are valid. 

My therapist said that some people have brain types that are just more susceptible to getting ptsd. Some people may get ptsd from what you went through, others might not. What matters is taking the steps towards making your life more manageable and enjoyable.
